title: PRIMARY KEY: Serial, Identity & UUIDs
description: Compare auto-incrementing SERIAL, modern GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY, UUIDv4, and UUIDv7 for primary keys.

data.text: A **PRIMARY KEY** uniquely identifies every record in a table and enforces both `UNIQUE` and `NOT NULL` constraints. In modern PostgreSQL, developers must decide between auto-incrementing integers and universally unique identifiers (UUIDs).

In PostgreSQL 10+, SQL-standard **`GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`** completely replaces legacy `SERIAL`. Identity columns prevent accidental manual overwrites of sequence numbers and integrate cleanly with schema permissions.

rows: High B-tree index fragmentation on large tables

data.title: Identity vs UUIDv4 Table Creation

data.text: What a Primary Key Actually Creates

Declaring `PRIMARY KEY` does three things: it adds `NOT NULL`, creates a `UNIQUE` btree index, and creates a constraint the planner can use for join elimination and for foreign key targets. Choosing the key type therefore affects storage, index size, and the write pattern of your busiest index.

data.title: Identity Columns: Behaviour and Pitfalls
data.content: `GENERATED ALWAYS` rejects explicit values; `BY DEFAULT` accepts them.

data.text: Random UUIDv4 values are not sequential, so each insert lands on a random page of the primary key index. That causes **page splits and cache misses** — the write amplification known as index bloat. Time-ordered UUIDv7 keeps the random uniqueness while sorting (roughly) by creation time, so inserts append to the right edge of the btree like a sequence does.

data.title: UUIDv7 on PostgreSQL 18+ and Earlier Versions
data.content: Check your version before you reach for a helper extension.

rows: `UUIDv7` (or a public id column plus an internal `BIGINT`)
Unguessable without the fragmentation of v4
Prefer a surrogate `BIGINT`/UUID with a `UNIQUE` on the natural key
Natural keys change; keys should be immutable

data.title: Interview Answer
data.text: Cover three points and you are done: (1) a primary key is a `UNIQUE NOT NULL` constraint backed by an index; (2) prefer `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` over `SERIAL` because it is SQL standard and owns its sequence; (3) prefer `UUIDv7` over `UUIDv4` when you need external, unguessable ids, because its time ordering avoids index fragmentation.

data.title: Measure UUID Fragmentation
data.description: See the cost of random keys for yourself.
steps: Create two tables with 1,000,000 rows: one `BIGINT IDENTITY`, one `UUID DEFAULT gen_random_uuid()`.
Compare `pg_total_relation_size` for both, including the primary key index.
Run `SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE id > ...` against both and compare buffers with `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.
Repeat with `uuidv7()` if your version supports it.
data.expectedOutcome: You can quantify why monotonic keys are cheaper, rather than repeating it as folklore.

items.question: Can a table have no primary key?
items.answer: Yes, but avoid it for entity tables. Without a primary key you cannot reference the table from a foreign key, and ORMs and replication tooling depend on one. Always add a unique key (primary or `UNIQUE NOT NULL`).

items.question: What is the difference between `PRIMARY KEY` and `UNIQUE NOT NULL`?
items.answer: Functionally similar for a single column, but a table may have only one primary key. Composite uniqueness is expressed with a `UNIQUE` constraint, and only the primary key defines the canonical row identity.

items.question: Should I use `BIGSERIAL` or `BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY`?
items.answer: Identity. It is standard SQL, the sequence is owned by the column, and permissions are simpler. `SERIAL` remains common in older codebases and is not wrong — just legacy.

items.question: Does a primary key stop gaps in the sequence?
items.answer: No. Rolled-back inserts and failed transactions consume sequence values, so gaps are normal and expected. Do not treat an id column as a count.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: `PRIMARY KEY` = `NOT NULL` + `UNIQUE` + a btree index; it is the target of every foreign key.
`GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` is the modern replacement for `SERIAL` and prevents accidental id overwrites.
`UUIDv4` is unguessable but random, which fragments indexes; `UUIDv7` (core in PG 18) keeps time ordering.
Prefer a surrogate key plus a `UNIQUE` constraint over using a mutable natural key as the primary key.
data.takeaway: State the trade-off, not a preference: sequential integers are fastest; time-ordered UUIDs are safe to expose.
